_convention._1_source_of_truth: en.json is THE source of truth for key names. fr.json mirrors this structure exactly — same keys, same nesting, same order. Never add a key to fr.json that does not exist here.
_convention._2_naming: Namespaced dot-paths, lowerCamelCase leaf names: <area>.<surface>.<element>. Examples: auth.login.title, auth.register.emailLabel, nav.dashboard, common.cancel, errors.invalidEmail.
_convention._3_areas: common.* = reused across two or more surfaces (buttons, field labels, generic words). auth.* = login / register / forgot-password. nav.* = navbar + account menu. errors.* = validation and failure messages. Add a new top-level area per surface group as later rounds land (dashboard.*, cv.*, interview.*).
_convention._4_no_duplicates: A string used on two surfaces lives in common.* and is referenced from both. Do NOT copy the same English text under two page keys — that is how translations drift apart.
_convention._5_fallback: Missing or empty keys fall back to English (fallbackLng: 'en', returnEmptyString: false). An untranslated surface renders English, never a blank or a raw key path — which is what lets translation ship surface by surface.
_convention._6_interpolation: Use named placeholders: "{{year}}", "{{label}}". escapeValue is false because React escapes already. NOTE: "count" is reserved by i18next for pluralization — a key using {{count}} MUST be declared as <key>_one / <key>_other in every locale (see nav.account.creditsLeft). Use a different placeholder name, e.g. {{n}}, when you do not want plural handling.
_convention._7_untranslated: Legal and billing copy (Terms of Service, Privacy Policy bodies) is deliberately NOT translated — it needs a qualified reviewer, not a best guess. See auth.register.legal.*.

problem.title: Why good candidates get rejected
problem.subcopy: Most rejections aren’t a human decision — they happen before anyone reads a word you wrote.
problem.stage2BodyLead: Scans for the exact keywords in the job description.
problem.stage3Body: Never happens — a person never sees your résumé.
problem.truthLead: It’s not your skills that get you rejected. It’s your
problem.whatIsAtsBody: Applicant Tracking Systems screen applications at 99% of Fortune 500 companies, filtering thousands automatically. If your résumé doesn’t exactly match the language of the job description, you’re filtered out before a human ever clicks “Open”.
problem.sprayBody: Sending the same generic CV to 100 jobs guarantees 100 rejections. Each job description is unique, with its own required skills and “magic words”.

fix.title: We tailor your CV for every single job.
fix.subcopy: Three moves that turn a generic résumé into one the software waves through.
fix.step1Body: Paste the job link. Our AI reads it like an ATS would, finding the critical keywords, skills, and requirements hidden in the text.
fix.step2Body: We don’t just add keywords. We rewrite your bullet points to highlight the relevant experience that matches this specific job.
fix.step3Body: You get a tailored PDF for that specific application. The ATS sees a 95%+ match, and your résumé lands on the recruiter’s desk.

tips.title: Keep the header clean and recruiter-ready
tips.intro: Your header is the first thing they see. A few small choices make a big difference.

list.0: Use a professional email — firstname.lastname@email.com beats a nickname.
list.1: City and country is enough — no need for a full street address.
list.2: Include your LinkedIn URL if you have one; recruiters click it.
list.3: Skip the photo unless you’re applying in a region where it’s standard.
list.4: Example: Jane Doe · London, UK · jane.doe@email.com · +44 7123 456 789 · linkedin.com/in/janedoe

history.title: Work history
history.subtitle: Your experience tells your professional story.

tips.title: Make every role count
tips.intro: Recruiters skim — your bullets do most of the work.

list.0: List your most recent role first, working backwards (reverse chronological).
list.1: Start each bullet with a strong action verb (Built, Led, Reduced, Launched).
list.2: Use the format Action + Context + Result — what you did, where, what changed.
list.3: Add concrete numbers wherever you can: team size, %, $, users, time saved.
list.4: Click ‘Ask Aria’ on any role and she’ll build or sharpen its bullets with you — drafted from what you actually did.

projects.title: Projects
projects.subtitle: Showcase your practical work and initiatives.

tips.title: Projects show what you do when nobody’s asking
tips.intro: Even small side projects matter — they show initiative.

list.0: Pick projects relevant to the role you’re targeting; cut the rest.
list.1: Each description: what it is, who used it, the most concrete outcome (users, downloads, impact).
list.2: If it was a team project, name your specific contribution — what you built or led.
list.3: Add a link if you have one — GitHub, live demo, write-up, anything.
list.4: Don’t list languages here — your Skills section already covers that.

projects.tip: Tip: 1-3 short bullets is enough. Lead with what it does, not how you built it.

education.title: Education
education.subtitle: Your academic background and qualifications.

tips.title: Keep education tight and relevant
tips.intro: Most readers spend a couple of seconds on this section.

list.0: List your most recent or highest qualification first.
list.1: Honors, GPA, or thesis only if it strengthens your application — otherwise skip it.
list.2: For experienced candidates (5+ years), education sits below work history.
list.3: Skip the high school once you have a degree — it’s implied.

education.certsDesc: Licences, certificates, and professional training — often the gating requirement for trades, operations, and healthcare roles.

skills.title: Skills
skills.subtitle: Highlight your expertise.

tips.title: Skills are scanned, not read
tips.intro: Recruiters and resume software (the systems recruiters use) match keywords here.

list.0: Mirror the language from the job description — exact wording matters.
list.1: Group related skills (Languages, Frameworks, Tools) so it’s scannable.
list.2: Lead with hard skills (tools, tech, languages); soft skills like “good communicator” need evidence elsewhere or skip them here.
list.3: List things you can confidently discuss in an interview — nothing more.
list.4: Aim for 15-25 total. Long lists dilute the strong ones.

bodyLanguage.heading: Walk in with presence
bodyLanguage.subtitle: How you show up speaks before you do. A few habits that read as confident:

0.title: The first 7 seconds
0.body: Impressions form almost instantly. Walk in with shoulders back, a warm smile, and unhurried, purposeful steps.

1.title: Posture
1.body: Sit tall with an open chest; lean in slightly when listening. Don’t shrink, slouch, or fold your arms.

2.title: Eye contact
2.body: Hold it ~4–5 seconds at a time — connection, not a stare. On video, look into the camera, not your own face.

3.title: Handshake & hands
3.body: If offered, a firm (not crushing) grip with a smile. Rest your hands calmly and let them gesture naturally.

4.title: Power pose
4.body: Two minutes standing tall, hands on hips, before you go in. It genuinely lifts confidence and lowers stress.

5.title: Voice & pace
5.body: Slow down. A breath before you answer beats filler words, and a calm, warm tone reads as confident.

calmKit.settleDesc: Slow, paced breathing lowers your heart rate and steadies your voice. Do this in the lobby or just before you join.
calmKit.reframeBody: Tell yourself “I’m excited”, not “I’m nervous.” It’s the same racing heart — but candidates who relabel it as excitement perform measurably better. The adrenaline is on your side.
calmKit.pictureBody: Take 20 seconds: see yourself walking in, a warm greeting, answering the first question calmly and clearly. Rehearsing success quiets the part of your brain that rehearses disaster.
calmKit.nightDesc: Decide everything tonight so the morning has zero stress to add.
